title: Introduction to Embedded Content
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of introduction to embedded content in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “Introduction to Embedded Content” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with what embedded content is, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Meaningful structure and metadata make content easier to navigate, understand, share, and maintain across different devices and assistive technologies.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Meaningful structure and metadata make content easier to navigate, understand, share, and maintain across different devices and assistive technologies.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Embedded content introduces a separate resource and sometimes a separate browsing context. Confirm the origin, disclose third-party dependencies, and restrict capabilities unless they are required.

items.title: What embedded content is
items.text: Embedded content introduces a separate resource and sometimes a separate browsing context. Confirm the origin, disclose third-party dependencies, and restrict capabilities unless they are required.

items.title: External versus locally hosted resources
items.text: Choose resource hints and loading behavior from measurement, not habit. Preserve intrinsic dimensions, avoid lazy-loading content needed immediately, and prioritize only genuinely important resources.

items.title: Browser handling of embedded documents
items.text: Embedded content introduces a separate resource and sometimes a separate browsing context. Confirm the origin, disclose third-party dependencies, and restrict capabilities unless they are required.

items.title: Embedded resources and page performance
items.text: Form controls need meaningful labels and names, clear instructions, and constraints that match the data. Treat browser validation as feedback for users, not proof that submitted data is trustworthy.

items.title: Privacy and security implications
items.text: Privacy and security implications is one of the decisions covered by Introduction to Embedded Content. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

content_blocks.code:
<iframe
  src="https://example.com/report"
  title="Public report preview"
  sandbox="allow-scripts"
  loading="lazy"
  width="800" height="500">
</iframe>
content_blocks.expected_output: The frame loads only if the URL permits embedding. Review the origin and grant sandbox permissions only when required.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in an .html file and open it in a modern browser. Inspect the result, then run an HTML validator if the lesson concerns syntax or structure. Example paths are illustrative; provide the referenced files or adjust paths before evaluating media/resource behavior.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the snippet in this lesson file or paste it into a fresh index.html file, then repeat the check.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Prefer the native semantic element that communicates intent. Do not choose markup solely for its default visual style.

content.task: Create a small HTML example that demonstrates introduction to embedded content. Keep the markup minimal, give every element a clear purpose, and inspect the rendered result.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Introduction to Embedded Content.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.
hints: Start with the smallest valid example for introduction to embedded content.
Add one element or attribute at a time, then check the result.
Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.
content.expected_output: The frame loads only if the URL permits embedding. Review the origin and grant sandbox permissions only when required.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

summary: Introduction to Embedded Content is about expressing document structure or behavior intentionally.

Privacy and security implications is one of the decisions covered by Introduction to Embedded Content. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.
Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
